title: America Now Wants Green Card Applicants to Leave the Country. Zoho's Founder Says They Should.
excerpt: A new USCIS policy redefines Adjustment of Status as 'extraordinary relief,' pushing H-1B holders into overseas processing. Sridhar Vembu's response: 'Please come home.'
body:
For years, Indian professionals on H-1B and L-1 visas treated Adjustment of Status as the standard path to a green card — a way to apply for permanent residence without leaving the country while their cases crawled through decade-long backlogs. On May 22, the US government told them that path is no longer standard.

US Citizenship and Immigration Services issued Policy Memorandum PM-602-0199, reclassifying Adjustment of Status as an "extraordinary form of relief." The practical effect: most temporary visa holders must now return to their home country and complete immigrant visa processing at a US embassy or consulate.

The Department of Homeland Security framed it as a return to legislative intent. "An alien who is in the US temporarily and wants a Green Card must return to their home country to apply," DHS said in a statement. "This policy allows our immigration system to function as the law intended instead of incentivizing loopholes."

## Vembu's Blunt Response

Sridhar Vembu, the billionaire founder of Zoho Corporation, weighed in the next day with a message that went viral in Indian tech circles. "Once again, my appeal to Indians in America on a visa. Please come home," he wrote on X on May 23. "Even if you feel it is hardship and sacrifice, self-respect should dictate your course. Let's make Bharat proud."

Vembu has long advocated building careers in India rather than abroad, but his remarks landed differently this time — against the backdrop of a policy that tangibly changes the calculus for every Indian professional with a pending green card. He argued that India's technology and startup base now offers opportunities that rival Silicon Valley, and that talent no longer needs to remain abroad by default.

"Bharat Mata needs your talent," he wrote.

## The Practical Damage

The new memorandum does more than change a bureaucratic pathway. It gives adjudicating officers broader discretion to deny applications, even when applicants meet formal legal requirements. Officers are now directed to weigh conduct "inconsistent with the purpose of the visa" — a phrase that adds uncertainty for people already in long employment-based queues.

The timing compounds the pain. The State Department's June 2026 Visa Bulletin moved sharply against Indian applicants in two core categories. EB-2 India retrogressed by 10.4 months to September 1, 2013, while EB-1 India moved back 3.5 months to December 15, 2022. For context, an EB-2 applicant from India whose priority date is today would be waiting for a green card based on a queue that is currently processing applications from 13 years ago.

Immigration lawyers warn of another hazard embedded in the shift to overseas processing. A person who departs the US after accumulating unlawful presence — even unintentionally, through visa processing delays — can trigger three-year or ten-year bars that block re-entry after the consular interview. Mixed-status households face separations lasting months or years while a principal applicant waits in India for an appointment.

"I can tell you that the new policy memo was, in my view, released in violation of the Administrative Procedures Act and I anticipate litigation will be quickly filed," said Greg Siskind, co-founder of immigration law firm Siskind Susser.

## A Reckoning for Indian Professionals

At least five US lawmakers have publicly criticised the rule. Arizona Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari called it "insanity" that would "separate families for months or even years." California Congressman Ted Lieu warned of "a significant exodus of top researchers, scientists, and industry leaders."

After backlash, USCIS revised its posture slightly, saying it would allow exceptions for applications that provide an "economic benefit or otherwise are in the national interest." But the policy language does not define either standard, leaving applicants in limbo.

For the tens of thousands of Indian professionals who have spent years — in some cases more than a decade — building lives and careers in the US while waiting for green cards, the question has become existential. Do they leave and risk the re-entry bars? Do they stay and hope for a legal challenge to succeed? Or do they take Vembu's advice and go home?

The answer may depend less on policy and more on whether India can absorb the talent it is being asked to reclaim.
